# Surucijātaka (Ja 489)

**ID:** Ja 489  
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Surucijātaka  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul13.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul13.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Surucijātaka* (Ja 489, PTS Ja IV 314ff.) is a canonical birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1887; Collins 2016]. According to its opening frame, the Buddha related the narrative while residing near Sāvatthī at the mansion of Migāra's mother (*Migāramātupāsāda*), occasioned by the eight boons granted to the lay disciple Visākhā [Fausböll 1887]. Set in Mithilā during the reign of King Suruci, the story of the past follows Prince Suruci (*Surucikumāro*), who travels to Takkasilā to acquire arts [Fausböll 1887]. In the narrative, a childless royal couple prays for a son; Sakka is stirred by Queen Sumedhā's prayer, questions her concerning her virtues, and grants her boon [Anandajoti 2010]. When a palace is planned for the royal prince, the king summons master geomancers (*vatthuvijjācariya*) to locate an auspicious construction site [Mus 1935]. In the story's resolution (*samodhāna*), Prince Mahāpanāda is identified with Bhaddaji, Queen Sumedhā with Visākhā, Vissakamma with Ānanda, and Sakka with the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1887].

The text has drawn attention from modern scholars for its treatment of domestic life, marital fidelity, and gender relations [Collins 2016; Cabezón 2017]. It is frequently cited as one of the few Buddhist narrative texts extolling monogamy, while also vividly portraying the misery and jealousy of co-wives (*sapattiyo*) as a distinctive hardship experienced by women in polygynous royal households [Collins 2016; Cabezón 2017]. The tale also extols the domestic ethics of a virtuous wife who behaves compassionately toward her husband, in-laws, co-wives, servants, and mendicants, promising earthly and celestial rewards for such virtues [Lewis & Tuladhar 2000].

- Passage-level parallels: Thig 2.7 Mittātherīgāthā; Ja 541 Nimijātaka; AN 3.37 Catumahārājasutta; AN 3.38 Dutiyacatumahārājasutta; SN 10.5 Sānusutta
- Mentioned in: Vv 15 Uttarāvimānavatthu; Vv 19 Lakhumāvimānavatthu; Vv 22 Bhadditthivimānavatthu; Vv 23 Soṇadinnāvimānavatthu; Vv 24 Uposathāvimānavatthu; Vv 25 Niddāvimānavatthu; Vv 37 Visālakkhivimānavatthu; Vv 52 Revatīvimānavatthu; Pv 39 Revatīpetavatthu

**Sources**

- [Anandajoti 2010] Bhikkhu Anandajoti, Buddhist Wisdom Verses: 551 verses from the Canon (2010) — Presents verse from Ja 489 and summarizes Sakka's test of the queen's virtue.
- [Collins 2016] Steven Collins, Readings of the Vessantara Jataka (2016) — Discusses PTS citation Ja IV 314ff., monogamy, co-wives' jealousy, and marital ethics.
- [Cabezón 2017] José Ignacio Cabezón, Sexuality in Classical South Asian Buddhism (2017) — Analyzes the Jātaka's praise of monogamy and maidenly choice.
- [Fausböll 1887] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka Together with Its Commentary, vol. 4 (1887) — Pali text of opening nidāna, story of the past in Mithilā, and the samodhāna.
- [Lewis & Tuladhar 2000] Todd Thornton Lewis and Labh Ratna Tuladhar, Popular Buddhist Texts from Nepal: Narratives and Rituals of Newar Buddhism (2000) — Notes moral rewards for virtuous wives treating co-wives and households compassionately.
- [Mus 1935] Paul Mus, Barabuḍur: Esquisse d'une histoire du bouddhisme fondée sur la critique archéologique des textes, part 2 — Cites the role of master geomancers (vatthuvijjācariya) in building the palace.
